Gig Review: Dark Alchemy VII – Aaron Stainthorpe / Dead Space Chamber Music / T.G. Edwards / Eldermother – St Thomas the Martyr, Bristol (19th September 2026)

Occasionally, an event comes along that produces absolutely zero hesitation in me before clicking that “buy tickets” button. Rarely, that event involves seven-plus hours of driving and a hotel stop along the way. Such is the power of the draw of this show.

Dark Alchemy is a collaborative project originally begun by Dead Space Chamber  Music (DSCM), with T.G. Edwards joining subsequently as a co-host. Together, they create dark and gothic musical events and experiences, making use of the crypts, chapels, churches, and other unique spaces around Bristol. The connection with Aaron Stainthorpe, and the invitation for him to rejoin the project here in Bristol, grew out of DSCM’s collaboration with him the previous year for a Darkher gig in Hebden Bridge.

The Church of St Thomas the Martyr is one such space. It is a late-eighteenth-century building attached to an even older tower and boasts a truly stunning exterior, including all of the gorgeous stained-glass windows and wooden furnishings you might expect of such a setting. Better still, it is currently a working church, used by a Roman Orthodox Parish and so, as we lucky goths sidle into the high-ceilinged space, stern icons and other liturgical items glint, half-hidden, in the sparse lighting.

Product Reviews & Price Comparisons

We all communicate in whispers as we find our spaces on the pews, shuffling along and chuckling almost nervously. Even if this were not a working place of worship, it feels as though we’ve entered into a sacred ritual space.

The ensemble of instruments at the front of the room – harp, cello, guitar, and microphone stands – are lit in unearthly tones by powerful LED light strips, their harsh glow diffused by a nearby smoke machine. The icons and murals of Christ and the saints almost appear to be judging the arrangement as the first act of the evening – Bristol-based Eldermother and her musicians – take their place by their respective instruments and microphones.

The band are elaborately turned out in beautiful gothic outfits and I feel underdressed in my travelling clothes – like I’ve snuck into a vampire’s masquerade or a dark elven wedding. This is no mere tavern  music. Many of the members are also veterans of black metal projects and it shows. Though this is a mostly acoustic set, the music is powerful and driven. Stunning twin vocals from two singers soar over a backdrop of folk-inspired classical fayre. Their cover of Sol Invictus’ “An English Garden (In the Rain)” is truly haunting and reverberates just enough (shout-out to sound-tech Rob Innel’s fantastic setup) through the pews and up to the rafters to bring a tear to even the driest eye.

After a round of applause there’s a short break, during which a few instruments are shuffled around and Eldermother are joined on the stage (or sanctuary, as it is normally used) by Dead Space Chamber Music (DSCM) for a surprise collaboration. It’s an evocative preview of DSCM’s set to come.

The instruments are moved aside and space is made in the centre of the sanctuary for T.G. Edwards’ modular synth. Sitting on the floor, Edwards twists and coaxes a dark, broody soundscape from the synth. I feel for those in the rows further back in the church as they won’t be able to see the artist’s hands at work. It is truly fascinating to watch him go: turning knobs, tapping buttons, and pushing sliders to shift pitch and frequency until the whole thing feels like a horror soundtrack. Deep, pulsing bass gives way to static, to clicks, and uncomfortably organic sounds. We are teased with a hint of rhythm, even some melody, before the growl and pulse returns. The entire church vibrates.

Metal (Music)

Dead Space Chamber Music begin their ceremony with vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Ellen Southern at the back of the church with a pair of hand cymbals. She moves rhythmically up the aisle past the enraptured audience, pausing to bring the cymbals together in time to the music.

Once she reaches the stage, we are treated to a spiritual performance of music that feels at once expertly performed and simultaneously spontaneous. Ellen reaches down at regular intervals to retrieve and play various small instruments. She seems to decide each instrument on the spot, and yet each addition is perfectly woven in with the backing cello, drums, and guitar. For one piece, Ellen wears a net veil over her head, her vocals ranging from mournful to manic and bright. She pours her soul out to us, baring powerful emotions as she performs. This is part art-piece, part song, and in this setting the emotional resonance of the music is amplified tenfold. At the set’s apotheosis, the singer carries a silver tray of rose petals that she distributes into the seated audience, stopping at each set of pews to toss handfuls over our heads. It feels like more than a gesture marking the end of a musical set. It feels like a blessing.

Music & Audio

Finally, Aaron Stainthorpe takes to the stage alongside the members of DSCM. T.G. Edwards returns with his synth, and over an improvised, brooding soundscape, Aaron recites some of his poetry.

It’s a delight for an old My Dying Bride fan like myself to discover that Aaron’s deep voice is just as – if not more – powerful in the flesh as it is on record. Though he could make a reading of the phone book sound intensely personal and important, his poems themselves are gorgeously lush. In concise lines, he creates haunting imagery which burrows itself into the shadows, to reside in the darkened corners behind the severe iconography of saviours and saints. It feels like a curse. We shiver in our pews, entranced.

One of the things I love about Aaron’s performance is that he always embodies the words he speaks or sings. His entire body shifts and his face contorts with the emotion of the piece. His fingers grasp at something we do not see, something we can only feel. After the poetry, we are treated to a series of deconstructed My Dying Bride songs – “deconstructed”, here, doing a lot of work, as the songs themselves would be indistinguishable were it not for Aaron’s signature vocals and the unforgettable lyrics.

Metal (Music)

“This is one you will all recognise,” he says, “maybe,” before launching into a bare-bones, acoustic(ish) version of “The Cry of Mankind”. I can barely suppress my happiness. I am a giddy fangirl.

Was it profound? Was it transcendent? Was I, ultimately, just a massive My Dying Bride fangirl who had travelled over seven hours to hear Aaron Stainthorpe read poetry in a church? Yes, yes, and yes. I’d do it again in a heartbeat.
